question:
Select the most appropriate option to substitute the underlined segment in the given sentence.
Rohan exercised and ate a lot, lest he should not be weak .
option_3: lest he would not be weak.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. lest he should be weak.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The conjunction "lest" itself means "so that... not" or "for fear that" — it already carries a negative sense.
◦ Rule: Lest + Subject + should + V1 (never add a separate "not" after "should", since "lest" is already negative in meaning).

• Applying the rule to the sentence: "Rohan exercised and ate a lot, lest he should be weak" means Rohan exercised and ate well so that he would NOT be weak. Adding another "not" after "should" (as in the original underlined segment) creates a double negative and is grammatically wrong.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "lest he should not weak" is incorrect on two counts — it wrongly repeats the negative "not" after "lest", and it drops the main verb "be" ("should not weak" is not a verb phrase).

• Option 2: "lest he would be weak" is incorrect because "lest" is always followed by "should" (or the base form/subjunctive), never by "would".

• Option 3: "lest he would not be weak." is incorrect for the same two reasons combined — it uses "would" instead of "should", and it wrongly retains the extra "not".

NOTE

• "Lest" can also be followed directly by the base form of the verb without "should": e.g. "Study hard lest you fail."

• Never use "not" or any other negative word (no, never) after "lest", as it is inherently negative in sense; this is one of the most frequently tested traps in SSC exams.

question:
Select the most appropriate ANTONYM for the underlined word in the given sentence.
Despite his annoyance, Rahul knew that rushing the delicate process would only lead to mistakes.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. Serenity.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word "Annoyance" means a feeling of slight anger or irritation. (चिड़चिड़ाहट/झुंझलाहट)
◦ Example: He could not hide his annoyance at being kept waiting.

• The antonym of "Annoyance" is "Serenity", which means the state of being calm, peaceful, and untroubled. (शांति)
◦ Example: She faced the crisis with remarkable serenity.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: Susceptibility (संवेदनशीलता): The quality of being likely to be affected by something; not opposite to annoyance.

• Option 2: Absurdity (बेतुकापन): The quality of being wildly unreasonable or illogical; unrelated in meaning to annoyance/calmness.

• Option 3: Gnawer: Not a standard English word in this sense ("gnaw" means to bite persistently); it is not an antonym of annoyance.

NOTE

• Other synonyms of "Annoyance": irritation, vexation, exasperation, displeasure.

• Other synonyms of "Serenity": calmness, tranquillity, composure, placidity.

question:
Select the most appropriate option that means the same as the underlined group of words to fill in the blank.
Most of the rivers dry up during the summer season, but the Ganga is full of water round the year because it is __________.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. perennial.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The underlined phrase "round the year" means continuing or existing throughout the whole year, without stopping.

• The word "Perennial" means lasting or existing all year round; continuing without interruption. (बारहमासी/वर्षभर बहने वाला)
◦ Example: The Ganga is a perennial river, unlike seasonal streams that dry up in summer.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "biennial" (द्विवार्षिक): Occurring every two years, or lasting for two years; does not mean "all year round".

• Option 2: "biannual" (अर्धवार्षिक): Occurring twice a year; does not match "round the year".

• Option 4: "annual" (वार्षिक): Occurring once every year; it describes frequency, not continuity throughout the year, so it does not convey "round the year".

NOTE

• Rivers that flow throughout the year (fed by glaciers/rain) are called "perennial rivers" (e.g. Ganga, Brahmaputra), while rivers that dry up in summer are called "seasonal/non-perennial rivers" (e.g. many peninsular rivers of India).

• Do not confuse: biennial (every 2 years) vs biannual (twice a year) — a commonly tested pair in SSC vocabulary.

question:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the given group of words.
On cloud nine
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Being very delighted.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The idiom "On cloud nine" means extremely happy or elated; in a state of blissful joy. (बहुत खुश/आनंदित)
◦ Example: When she got the scholarship, she was on cloud nine for the whole day.

• The idiom is believed to originate from an old classification of clouds, where "cloud nine" (cumulonimbus) was described as the highest and fluffiest cloud — being on it suggested being on top of the world.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: Being angry with someone is not related; anger is expressed by idioms like "to see red" or "to fly off the handle".

• Option 3: Flying in the sky is a literal misreading of "cloud"; the idiom is figurative, not literal.

• Option 4: Being very high takes "cloud" literally (in the sky) rather than as a figurative expression of intense happiness.

NOTE

• Other idioms of happiness often asked in SSC: "Over the moon", "Walking on air", and "In seventh heaven" — all mean extremely happy.

• Contrast with idioms of sadness: "Down in the dumps", "In low spirits".

question:
Select the correct spelling to fill in the blank.
When numerous ideas are presented in a historical context, more than mere _____ can be seen.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. parallelism.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The correct spelling is "Parallelism" — the state of being parallel, or correspondence/similarity between things being compared. (समानता/समांतरता)
◦ Example: The historian noted a striking parallelism between the two revolutions.

• Spelling key: PARA + LLEL + ISM. Note the double "L" in the middle ("-llel-") and the ending "-ism", derived from "parallel" + "-ism".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "paralialism" — incorrect; an extra "i" has been wrongly inserted after "paral".

• Option 3: "paralelism" — incorrect; only a single "l" is used in "paralel", whereas the correct word has a double "ll".

• Option 4: "parollelism" — incorrect; the second vowel has been wrongly changed from "a" to "o" ("parol-" instead of "paral-").

NOTE

• Remember the root word "parallel" (two straight lines equidistant apart) — most spelling errors in "parallelism" involve the double "l" being dropped or the vowels being swapped.

• Other commonly confused double-letter spellings in SSC exams: occurrence, embarrass, harass, committee, questionnaire.

question:
Parts of a sentence are given below in jumbled order. Arrange the parts in the correct order to form a meaningful sentence.
A. So I am not very sure
B. I have a driving license
C. Of myself reaching home safely
D. But no real driving experience
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. BDAC.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• To arrange jumbled parts correctly, first identify the part that can independently begin the sentence (with a clear subject and main verb), then trace the logical chain of ideas (cause, contrast, and result) that follows it.

• Part B ("I have a driving license") is the only part with a complete subject-verb-object structure, so it must begin the sentence.

• Part D ("But no real driving experience") logically follows B, introducing a contrast ("license" but no "experience") using "but".

• Part A ("So I am not very sure") follows as the result of having no real experience, introduced by "so".

• Part C ("Of myself reaching home safely") completes the sentence, specifying what the speaker is "not very sure" of.

◦ Full sentence: "I have a driving license but no real driving experience, so I am not very sure of myself reaching home safely."

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3 (BDAC).

Additional Information

• Option 1 (BCAD) is incorrect because it places C ("of myself reaching home safely") immediately after B, which breaks the logical link between "license" and the contrasting "no real driving experience".

• Option 2 (BDCA) is incorrect because it places C before A, resulting in "...no real driving experience of myself reaching home safely so I am not very sure", which is not meaningful.

• Option 4 (CABD) is incorrect because it begins with C, which cannot stand as an opening part since it has no subject of its own and depends on what precedes it.

NOTE

• In parajumbles, always look first for the part that can grammatically and logically stand as the opening sentence (a clear subject + verb), and then use connecting words ("but", "so", "of") as clues to link the remaining parts.

• Contrast connectors like "but" and result connectors like "so" are strong indicators of sequence in such questions.

question:
Select the correctly spelt word to fill in the blank.
Calder Hall is a nuclear power station in England which is known as the first nuclear power station to generate electricity for ___________ purposes.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. commercial.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The correct spelling is "Commercial" — relating to trade, business, or profit-making activity. (वाणिज्यिक)
◦ Example: The power station started generating electricity for commercial purposes in 1956.

• Spelling key: COM + MER + CIAL. Note the double "m" ("comm-") and the ending "-cial", not "-cail" or "-ceil".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "comercial" — incorrect; the double "m" has been wrongly reduced to a single "m".

• Option 2: "comercail" — incorrect; besides the missing double "m", the ending has been wrongly written as "-cail" instead of "-cial".

• Option 3: "commerceil" — incorrect; the ending "-cial" has been wrongly replaced with "-ceil".

NOTE

• Related words: commerce (noun), commercially (adverb), commercialise (verb).

• Other words commonly misspelt with double consonants in SSC exams: accommodate, occurrence, recommend, embarrass.

question:
Select the option that expresses the given sentence in passive voice.
Can you compose an inspiring poem?
option_1: Can an inspiring poem be composed?
option_2: An inspiring poem can be composed by you.
option_3: Can an inspiring poem be composed by you?
option_4: Can an inspiring poem by you composed?
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Can an inspiring poem be composed by you?

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence "Can you compose an inspiring poem?" is an interrogative sentence with the modal "can", in the Simple Present Tense.

• Rule — Interrogative sentences with modals (Simple Present):
◦ Active: Can/Could/Will + Subject + V1 + Object?
◦ Passive: Can/Could/Will + Object + be + V3 + by + Subject?

• Applying the rule: the object "an inspiring poem" becomes the subject; the modal "can" stays at the start; the verb "compose" becomes "be composed"; and "you" becomes the agent with "by".
◦ Passive: Can an inspiring poem be composed by you?

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1 is incorrect because the agent "by you" has been dropped, changing the meaning of the sentence.

• Option 2 is incorrect because it is framed as a statement ("can be composed"), not as a question, whereas the original sentence is interrogative and must remain a question in the passive.

• Option 4 is incorrect because the word order is wrong — "by you composed" should be "be composed by you"; the past participle must come immediately after "be".

NOTE

• In passive questions with modals, the question mark and the interrogative structure (modal + subject/object + verb) must be preserved.

• The agent ("by + doer") may be dropped only when it is unimportant or unknown, never as a default choice when the original sentence specifies it.

question:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the given word.
Pugnacious
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. Waspish.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word "Pugnacious" means eager or quick to argue, quarrel, or fight; aggressively combative. (झगड़ालू)
◦ Example: His pugnacious attitude made him unpopular with his colleagues.

• "Waspish" means quick to show anger or irritation; sharp-tongued and easily provoked, which is the closest match to the combative, quarrelsome sense of "pugnacious" among the given options. (चिड़चिड़ा/तीखे स्वभाव वाला)

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: Impatient (अधीर): Unable to wait calmly; refers to a lack of patience, not a tendency to fight.

• Option 2: Good-tempered (सौम्य स्वभाव): Calm and even-tempered — this is actually opposite in sense to "pugnacious".

• Option 3: Arrogant (अहंकारी): Having an exaggerated sense of one's own importance; describes pride, not combativeness.

NOTE

• Other words meaning quarrelsome/combative often asked in SSC: belligerent, bellicose, contentious, cantankerous, quarrelsome.

• Do not confuse "pugnacious" (fond of fighting) with the similar-sounding "pungent" (sharp in smell/taste) — they are unrelated words.

question:
Select the most appropriate synonym of the given word.
Condone
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Pardon.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word "Condone" means to accept and allow an offence or wrongdoing to continue; to forgive or overlook something. (क्षमा करना/माफ करना)
◦ Example: The manager refused to condone such careless behaviour at work.

• "Pardon" means to forgive or excuse someone for a fault or offence, which matches the meaning of "condone" closely. (क्षमा करना)

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: Solicitude (चिंता/सरोकार): Care or concern for someone's wellbeing; unrelated to forgiving an offence.

• Option 2: Penalty (दंड): A punishment for breaking a rule; this is actually opposite in sense to "condone".

• Option 4: Solace (सांत्वना): Comfort received after a loss or disappointment; unrelated to forgiving wrongdoing.

NOTE

• Other synonyms of "condone": overlook, excuse, forgive, disregard.

• Do not confuse "condone" (to forgive an offence) with "condemn" (to strongly disapprove of) — they are near-opposites and are a common SSC trap.

question:
Select the most appropriate synonym of the given word.
Tendency
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Proneness.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word "Tendency" means an inclination to act or think in a particular way; a natural disposition towards something. (झुकाव/प्रवृत्ति)
◦ Example: He has a tendency to procrastinate.

• "Proneness" means the state of being likely to do, suffer from, or be affected by something; a natural inclination, which matches "tendency" closely. (झुकाव/प्रवृत्ति)

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: Distaste (अरुचि): A feeling of dislike; unrelated to a natural inclination.

• Option 2: Decoy (प्रलोभन/चारा): Something used to lure or trap; unrelated in meaning.

• Option 4: Aversion (विमुखता): A strong dislike or unwillingness towards something — the opposite of an inclination, not a synonym of "tendency".

NOTE

• Other synonyms of "tendency": inclination, propensity, disposition, leaning.

• Do not confuse "tendency" (inclination towards) with "aversion" (dislike/turning away from) — they are near-opposites and are frequently tested together.

question:
Select the option that expresses the given sentence in passive voice.
The tutor was not teaching the student.
option_1: The student was teaching the tutor.
option_2: The student was not taught by the tutor.
option_3: The student was not being taught by the tutor.
option_4: The student was not being teaching by the tutor.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. The student was not being taught by the tutor.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence "The tutor was not teaching the student" is a negative sentence in the Past Continuous Tense.

• Rule — Past Continuous Tense:
◦ Active: Subject + was/were + not + V-ing + Object
◦ Passive: Object + was/were + not + being + V3 + by + Subject

• Applying the rule: the object "the student" becomes the subject; the auxiliary "was" is retained (singular subject); the verb "teaching" becomes "being taught"; and "the tutor" becomes the agent with "by".
◦ Passive: The student was not being taught by the tutor.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1 is incorrect because the subject and object have been wrongly interchanged, reversing the meaning of the sentence entirely.

• Option 2 is incorrect because "was not taught" is the passive form of the Simple Past Tense, not the Past Continuous Tense used in the original sentence.

• Option 4 is incorrect because "being teaching" is an ungrammatical form; the passive of a continuous tense always uses the past participle (V3), i.e. "being taught", never "being teaching".

NOTE

• The passive of continuous tenses always follows the pattern "being + V3" (e.g. is being done, was being written) — never "being + V-ing".

• Continuous tenses (Present/Past Continuous) do not have a passive form in the Perfect Continuous or Future Continuous aspects — only Present Continuous and Past Continuous can be converted to passive voice.

question:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the given group of words.
A bitter pill
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Facing a distressing situation.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The idiom "A bitter pill (to swallow)" means an unpleasant fact or situation that is difficult to accept, but must be accepted nonetheless. (कड़वा सच/कठिन स्थिति स्वीकारना)
◦ Example: Losing the championship after such hard work was a bitter pill for the team to swallow.

• The idiom draws on the image of medicine that tastes bitter but must be swallowed for one's own good — representing something painful that must nonetheless be endured or accepted.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: Talking nonsense is unrelated; nonsense talk is better expressed by idioms like "to talk through one's hat".

• Option 3: Arguing unnecessarily is unrelated to accepting an unpleasant truth.

• Option 4: Getting furious easily describes a short temper, not the idea of enduring something unpleasant.

NOTE

• Other idioms of accepting hardship often asked in SSC: "To grin and bear it", "To bite the bullet", and "To face the music".

• Contrast: "A blessing in disguise" — something that seems bad at first but turns out to be beneficial.

question:
Select the most appropriate option that can substitute the underlined word in the given sentence.
Bankrupts are those who are incapable to pay their debts.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. incompetent.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word "Incapable" means not having the ability, competence, or capacity to do something. (असमर्थ/अक्षम)
◦ Example: Bankrupts are those who are incapable of paying their debts.

• "Incompetent" means lacking the necessary skill or ability to do something properly, which is the closest match among the given options to "incapable" in the sense of lacking the ability (here, financial ability) to pay debts. (अक्षम/असमर्थ)

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "capable" (सक्षम): Means having the ability to do something — this is the direct opposite of "incapable", not a substitute.

• Option 2: "powerful" (शक्तिशाली): Means having great power or strength; unrelated to the idea of lacking the ability to pay debts.

• Option 4: "meagre" (अपर्याप्त/तुच्छ): Means small or lacking in quantity; describes an amount, not a lack of ability.

NOTE

• Other synonyms of "incapable": unable, unfit, incompetent, powerless.

• Do not confuse "incapable" (lacking ability) with "incapacitated" (made unable to function, usually due to illness/injury) — both share the root "capa-" (from Latin capax, able to hold).

question:
Parts of a sentence are given below in jumbled order. Select the option that arranges the parts in the correct sequence to form a meaningful sentence.
(P) dreams provide an escape
(Q) where reality is suspended
(R) into a world
(O) of endless possibilities
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. PROQ.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• To arrange jumbled parts correctly, identify the part with a clear subject and main verb to begin the sentence, then trace how each subsequent phrase logically modifies the one before it.

• Part P ("dreams provide an escape") has a complete subject-verb-object structure, so it must begin the sentence.

• Part R ("into a world") logically follows P, specifying where the "escape" leads to.

• Part O ("of endless possibilities") follows R, describing what kind of "world" is being referred to.

• Part Q ("where reality is suspended") completes the sentence, further describing the "world of endless possibilities".

◦ Full sentence: "Dreams provide an escape into a world of endless possibilities where reality is suspended."

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2 (PROQ).

Additional Information

• Option 1 (OPQR) is incorrect because it begins with O ("of endless possibilities"), which cannot stand as an opening phrase since it has no subject of its own.

• Option 3 (QORP) is incorrect because it begins with Q ("where reality is suspended"), which is a subordinate clause that cannot open the sentence meaningfully.

• Option 4 (RPOQ) is incorrect because it places R ("into a world") before P ("dreams provide an escape"), leaving "into a world" without a preceding verb to attach to.

NOTE

• In parajumbles, phrases beginning with prepositions ("into", "of") or relative adverbs ("where") almost never open a sentence — they follow a main clause.

• Always locate the part with the complete subject + verb + object first, as it anchors the correct sequence.

question:
The following sentence has been split into segments. Identify the segment that contains an error. If you don't find any error, mark 'No error' as your answer.
People admired him, for / he lived by the same principals / that he preached.
option_3: he lived by the same principals
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. he lived by the same principals.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The error lies in the word "principals", which is a homophone mistake. In this sentence, the intended meaning is "principles" — meaning rules or standards of good behaviour, or fundamental truths/beliefs one lives by.

• "Principal" (with an "a") means the head of a school/institution, or something of chief/primary importance, which does not fit the context of "living by" something.

• Corrected segment: "he lived by the same principles" — meaning he practised the same values/beliefs that he preached to others.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1 ("that he preached") is grammatically and contextually correct as it stands.

• Option 2 ("No error") is incorrect because segment 3 does contain a clear spelling/word-choice error ("principals" instead of "principles").

• Option 4 ("People admired him, for") is grammatically correct; "for" is correctly used here as a conjunction meaning "because".

NOTE

• Principal vs Principle is one of the most commonly tested homophone pairs in SSC exams: "principal" = head of an institution / main, chief (adjective); "principle" = a rule, law, or fundamental truth (noun).
◦ Memory tip: "The princiPAL is my PAL" (both end in "-pal"); "a princiPLE is a ruLE" (both end in "-le").

• Other commonly confused homophones in SSC: stationary/stationery, complement/compliment, affect/effect.

question:
Select the most appropriate ANTONYM of the given word.
Dogmatic
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Liberal.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word "Dogmatic" means inclined to lay down principles or opinions as incontrovertibly true, without allowing for debate; rigidly opinionated. (हठधर्मी/कट्टर)
◦ Example: His dogmatic approach to teaching left no room for students' questions.

• The antonym of "Dogmatic" is "Liberal", which means open to new ideas and willing to respect or accept behaviour or opinions different from one's own; broad-minded. (उदार/खुले विचारों वाला)

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: Concerned (चिंतित): Worried or interested about something; unrelated to open-mindedness.

• Option 3: Conservative (रूढ़िवादी): Holding traditional values and resistant to change — this is actually close in meaning to "dogmatic", not its opposite.

• Option 4: Diplomatic (कूटनीतिक): Tactful in dealing with others; does not specifically mean open-minded about opinions/beliefs.

NOTE

• Other synonyms of "Dogmatic": opinionated, rigid, inflexible, doctrinaire.

• Other antonyms of "Dogmatic": open-minded, flexible, broad-minded, tolerant.

question:
Select the most appropriate synonym of the given word.
Kilter
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Order.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word "Kilter" means a state of proper or good working condition (usually used in the phrase "in kilter" or "out of kilter"). (व्यवस्थित/ठीक स्थिति)
◦ Example: The old machine was out of kilter and needed repair; once fixed, it was back in kilter.

• "Order" means a state in which everything is functioning correctly or arranged properly, which matches the meaning of "kilter" (in good working condition). (व्यवस्था)

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: Disrepair (जीर्ण अवस्था): A state of disorder or bad condition due to neglect; this is actually the opposite of "kilter".

• Option 3: Anarchy (अराजकता): A state of disorder due to absence of authority; opposite in sense to "kilter".

• Option 4: Shambles (अस्त-व्यस्त स्थिति): A state of total disorder or confusion; opposite in sense to "kilter".

NOTE

• The phrase "out of kilter" means not working properly / out of order, while "in kilter" means working properly.

• Options 2, 3, and 4 (Disrepair, Anarchy, Shambles) are all synonyms of "disorder", making them antonyms — not synonyms — of "kilter"; be careful not to confuse the direction of meaning in such questions.

question:
The given sentence is divided into four segments. Select the option that has the segment with a grammatical error.
We were on the way/ to the party;/ suddenly, there/ will a heavy downpour.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. will a heavy downpour.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence begins with "We were on the way", which is in the Past Tense. For consistency (tense concord), every clause in the sentence must remain in the past tense unless there is a specific reason to shift.

• Rule — Tense Consistency: When narrating past events, all verbs describing simultaneous or connected actions in the same sentence must stay in the same (past) tense, and the sentence must have a proper verb structure ("there + was/were + Noun").

• The segment "will a heavy downpour" is faulty on two counts — it wrongly uses the future modal "will" instead of the past form "was", and it is missing the linking verb altogether ("there will a heavy downpour" is not grammatical even in the future tense; it should be "there will BE a heavy downpour").
◦ Corrected: "...suddenly, there was a heavy downpour."

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1 ("to the party;") is grammatically correct as it stands.

• Option 2 ("We were on the way") is grammatically correct; it correctly sets the sentence in the Past Continuous/Past tense.

• Option 4 ("suddenly, there") is grammatically correct; "there" is correctly used as an introductory/dummy subject before a verb of existence.

NOTE

• The structure "there + be (is/am/are/was/were) + Subject" is used to indicate existence; it must always include a form of "be", never a bare modal like "will" without "be".

• Tense-consistency errors (mixing past and future/present within one narrative sentence) are one of the most frequently tested error types in SSC error-spotting questions.

question:
Select the option that can substitute/replace the bracketed word correctly and complete the sentence.
He (seek) for the wallet in his pocket.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Sought.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence describes a single, completed action referring to a specific past occasion ("He ___ for the wallet in his pocket"), which requires the Simple Past Tense.

• Rule — Simple Past Tense: Subject + V2 (past form of the verb) + Object. The past form of the irregular verb "seek" is "sought" (seek – sought – sought).

• Applying the rule: "He sought for the wallet in his pocket" correctly places the verb "seek" in its simple past form to match the context of a completed action.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "Had seeking" is incorrect; "had" (Past Perfect auxiliary) must be followed by the past participle (V3), i.e. "had sought", not the "-ing" form.

• Option 3: "Are seeking" is incorrect; "are" is a plural/present auxiliary and does not agree with the singular subject "He", nor does it fit the past context.

• Option 4: "Seeking" is incorrect on its own, as a bare "-ing" form cannot function as the main finite verb of the sentence without an auxiliary ("is/was seeking").

NOTE

• "Seek" is an irregular verb: seek – sought – sought.

• Other commonly tested irregular verbs with similar "-ought/-aught" past forms: buy – bought – bought, catch – caught – caught, teach – taught – taught, think – thought – thought.

question:
In the following passage, some words have been deleted. Read the passage carefully and select the most appropriate option to fill in each blank.

This Diwali is more significant because we are going to celebrate it after three years, without the evil shadow of Covid-19 that (1)_________ looming over all festivities. The lockdowns and endless bad news of death and (2)_________ had turned our country into a zone of gloom. But, this season of Diwali (3)_________ all the sorrows of people by lighting the candle of hope in their lives. We can see the lights, the candles, the lanterns, and the busy people coming out of their houses and purchasing toys for their children. Let's (4)_________ those people who have made such a huge contribution to (5)_________ good thoughts and saving people's lives.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 1.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. was.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The blank requires a verb to complete the relative clause **"the evil shadow of Covid-19 that ___ looming over all festivities"**, which needs an auxiliary verb to go with the present participle "looming" to form the Past Continuous Tense.

• Rule — Past Continuous Tense (Subject-Verb Agreement): A singular subject takes "was", while a plural subject takes "were". Here, the subject of the relative clause is "that", referring back to the singular noun "shadow", so the singular auxiliary "was" is required.

• Additionally, the passage recalls a period now in the past (before this Diwali, three years ago), so the past tense "was" is required rather than the present tense "is/are".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "is" is incorrect; it is present tense and also does not agree with the past time frame of the passage.

• Option 2: "were" is incorrect; it does not agree with the singular subject "shadow" (that).

• Option 3: "are" is incorrect; it is present tense (plural) and fits neither the singular subject nor the past time frame.

NOTE

• In Past Continuous Tense, the auxiliary must agree in number with the subject: was (singular) / were (plural), followed by the V-ing form.

• Reading the full passage for time clues (here, "after three years", referring to the pandemic period) is essential to correctly choose between present and past tense options in cloze passages.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The blank completes the phrase **"The lockdowns and endless bad news of death and ___ had turned our country into a zone of gloom", which requires a word that logically pairs with "death"** as a source of "bad news" during the pandemic.

• "Disease" (referring to Covid-19 illness) fits logically with "death", since news of rising infections/illness alongside deaths was what caused widespread gloom during the pandemic.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "demonetisation" is incorrect; it refers to a specific economic policy event unrelated to the pandemic context of "death and ___" described here.

• Option 4: "new birth" is incorrect; new birth is a positive, hopeful event, the opposite of the "gloom" described in the sentence.

NOTE

• In cloze passages, always check that the chosen word matches both the grammatical fit and the overall tone/context (here, negative and pandemic-related) of the surrounding sentence.

• Contextual pairing ("death and disease") is a common collocation tested in comprehension-based cloze questions.

solution_text:

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The blank completes the sentence **"this season of Diwali ___ all the sorrows of people by lighting the candle of hope in their lives", which requires a verb meaning "to get rid of" or "to cast off"** the sorrows.

• "Has shed" (from "shed", meaning to cast off or discard) fits the context, as it conveys that this Diwali season has removed/cast off people's sorrows through hope. The Present Perfect Tense ("has + V3") is appropriate here since it links a past action (the arrival of hope this Diwali) to its continuing present relevance/result.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "had recognised" is incorrect; "recognised" (to acknowledge/identify) does not fit the meaning of removing sorrows, and the Past Perfect tense does not match the passage's time frame.

• Option 2: "has hovered" is incorrect; "hovered" (to stay suspended in one place) does not convey the sense of removing sorrows — it would suggest sorrows persisting, contrary to the hopeful meaning intended.

• Option 4: "has adopted" is incorrect; "adopted" (to take up/accept) does not fit logically with "sorrows" being adopted, which would contradict the positive meaning of the sentence.

NOTE

• "Shed" as a verb (shed – shed – shed, irregular, same form in all tenses) means to get rid of or discard, e.g. "shed light on", "shed tears", "shed old habits".

• Present Perfect Tense ("has/have + V3") is used for a past action whose effect/result continues to be relevant in the present — apt for describing how this Diwali's hopeful mood has removed lingering pandemic-era sorrow.

solution_text:

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The blank completes the sentence **"Let's ___ those people who have made such a huge contribution to spreading good thoughts and saving people's lives", which requires a word meaning "to honour or praise"** those people.

• "Salute" means to honour, praise, or pay respect to someone for their achievement or contribution, which fits the positive, appreciative tone of the sentence describing people who helped others during the pandemic. (सलाम करना/सम्मान करना)

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "berate" is incorrect; it means to scold or criticise angrily, which contradicts the appreciative tone of the sentence.

• Option 3: "terminate" is incorrect; it means to end or stop something, which does not fit the sense of honouring people's contribution.

• Option 4: "onerous" is incorrect; it is an adjective meaning burdensome, not a verb, and cannot grammatically fit the blank ("Let's onerous those people" is ungrammatical).

NOTE

• "Salute" is commonly used figuratively (beyond its literal military sense) to mean "to honour or commend" someone's efforts, e.g. "We salute the courage of our frontline workers."

• Other words meaning to honour/praise: commend, applaud, laud, extol — all common in SSC vocabulary-in-context questions.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The blank completes the sentence **"...those people who have made such a huge contribution to ___ good thoughts and saving people's lives", which requires a word meaning "to disseminate or propagate"** good thoughts.

• "Spreading" means circulating or making something known or reach more people, which fits the sense of good thoughts being shared widely, in parallel with "saving people's lives" as another positive contribution mentioned in the same sentence.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "stagnating" is incorrect; it means becoming stagnant or failing to develop/progress, which contradicts the positive act of sharing good thoughts.

• Option 2: "impeding" is incorrect; it means obstructing or hindering, the opposite of promoting good thoughts.

• Option 3: "implicating" is incorrect; it means involving someone in a crime or wrongdoing, which is irrelevant and negative in this positive context.

NOTE

• "Spread" (spread – spread – spread) is commonly used with abstract nouns like "spreading awareness", "spreading positivity", "spreading good thoughts" — a frequent collocation in comprehension passages.

• In cloze passages, always check for parallel structure — here, "contribution to spreading good thoughts AND saving people's lives" shows two parallel positive contributions joined by "and".
